headline: New moon springs load up Plum Gut as fluke push out of the bays
subhead: Big tides building for the weekend flood, and the current lines from Horton Point to Orient are starting to show life again.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it usually does the week after a full moon — it settled down. Current went slack in the middle of the tide cycle, the wind sat out of the southwest most days and pushed a little chop against the north-facing beaches, and the water along my stretch held steady, not cold, not blazing, just working its way toward summer temperature the way it does every July. Nothing dramatic happened, and that's fine by me. Slack water after a full moon usually means the fish stop chasing bait around and start digesting it, which is exactly what I saw — a lot of marks on the fish finder sitting tight to bottom structure at Rocky Point and not doing much about anything you threw at them.

That's about to change. We're sliding into a new moon this weekend, and new moon means spring tides — the biggest swings of the month. More water moving through Plum Gut, more current stacking up against Orient Point, more push through the Race. That current is the engine for everything out here. When it starts ripping again, bait gets displaced off the flats and funneled into the rips, and the bass and blues that have been holding deep and lazy start working the seams. The window everybody ought to have circled is Friday through Monday, the tenth through the thirteenth — the peak of the spring tide lines up with the evening flood, which puts a strong push of water moving into the Gut right around sunset. That's the first real PM window we've had since the June full moon, and it's the kind of setup that gets stripers moving up into the current lanes to feed instead of just holding under it.

On the fluke side, the story this month has been bay water running warm — warm enough that fluke have been sliding out of the back bays and into anything with moving, cooler water: inlets, channels, current-scoured bottom. Mattituck Inlet has been the beneficiary. Guys working the outgoing tide right off the jetty rocks with three-quarter-ounce bucktails and white Gulp Swimming Mullets have been finding keeper fluke stacked in that deeper cut where the inlet dumps into the Sound — nothing gaudy, but a few fish in the 20 to 22-inch range mixed with a lot of shorts that need to get thrown back. Slow-drag it right along bottom on the drop, and don't be afraid to tip the bucktail with a strip of squid when the current's really moving; the scent seems to matter more when the water's a little stirred up.

Bluefish have been scattered but present — small to mid-size blues showing up in blitzes off Horton Point and Rocky Point early and late in the day, chasing bunker pods that have been thick along that stretch. Nothing sustained, more like fifteen-minute windows where the water turns to white foam and then goes quiet again. If you see the gulls diving, get on it fast — diamond jigs, an ounce and a half, silver or chartreuse, worked fast through the melee, or a topwater popper if you want the visual. Don't waste time on a spot once the birds lift off; they don't come back for round two out here most days.

Stripers have been the tougher nut. A few fish have come off the boulder fields near Rocky Point on live eels fished on the bottom during the last two hours of the outgoing, and there's been better action right at the mouth of Plum Gut itself for guys willing to work bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig in the deeper water where the current really funnels. But it's been a fish here, a fish there — not a pattern you can set your watch by. I expect that to sharpen up with the new moon current. When that Gut starts ripping the way it does on a big tide, bass stack up in the eddies behind the rocks and feed hard for a short window right at the peak of the flood and again on the first hour of the drop. That's when I'll be out there, working bucktails tipped with pork rind along the seams, letting the jig fall into the slack pockets behind structure rather than fighting the main current.

Porgies have been steady and reliable if unspectacular — small to medium scup off the Orient breakwalls and around the rock piles near the Point, taking sandworms and pieces of green crab fished on a simple high-low rig in fifteen to twenty-five feet. Good action for anybody who wants a guaranteed bend in the rod without a lot of running around. Blackfish are out of season on this stretch through the summer, so leave the crabs for the porgies and save the tog game plan for when the water cools and the fall opener rolls around — I'll be scouting rock piles for that starting in September like I do every year.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, have been a non-event. The water's warm enough on paper, but warm water alone doesn't make weakfish show up, and I haven't heard of a single one taken along this whole stretch this year. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

For the week ahead: if the wind stays reasonable and doesn't blow hard out of the north, I'd fish the Friday and Saturday evening flood at Plum Gut and right off Orient Point, working the current seams as the spring tide builds toward its peak. That's where I'd put my money. Backup plan is the Mattituck Inlet fluke drift on the outgoing if the bass don't cooperate — that fishery's been the most consistent thing going, and consistent beats exciting most weeks out here.
